title: Methods
text:
mcPHASES v1.0.0 on PhysioNet, restricted access under the PhysioNet Restricted Health Data License. Interval 2022: 42 participants in Toronto, about three months each, with a Fitbit Sense (nightly wrist temperature, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep breathing rate, sleep), a Dexcom G6 continuous glucose monitor, Mira urinary LH and E3G with a four-phase label per day, and a daily symptom diary on a 0–5 scale. The 2024 return interval is held out and has not been used.

    M --> P[Paired within participant<br/>Menstrual, Fertility, Luteal − Follicular]
    P --> E[Paired mean difference and Hedges' g<br/>95 % BCa, 5,000 participant resamples]
    Q --> C[Closed cycles from menstrual onsets<br/>in the phase labels, 10–60 days]
    C --> A[Three-level REML model of daily values<br/>person, cycle and day components of the luteal contrast]

    V --> D[Distance-based repeatability R_vec]

title: Methods
text:
Statistics

Cohort shifts. DABEST paired mean difference and Hedges’ g with 95 % bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap intervals over participants (5,000 resamples). Native units are primary; g only to compare cells across metrics.
Persistence of a person’s contrast. Per device metric, a linear mixed model of daily values fitted by REML (statsmodels): fixed luteal indicator; participant random intercept and luteal slope (correlated); cycle-within-participant intercept and luteal-slope variance components; day residuals. The between-person SD of the luteal slope is the quantity of interest: repeatability of a random slope in the sense of Araya-Ajoy et al. (2015) and Schielzeth & Nakagawa (2022), within the general repeatability framework of Nakagawa & Schielzeth (2010). Fits whose person intercept–slope correlation is ±1 are reported as singular and uninformative. Bootstrap intervals for the variance components are withheld because a variance at its boundary makes them invalid; calibrated inference by simulating the null on the same design, after Crainiceanu & Ruppert (2004), is in progress.
Vector repeatability. Each closed cycle’s five-metric contrast is divided per metric by the total SD of cycle contrasts; R_vec = 1 − mean squared within-person distance / mean squared between-person distance over the 22 participants with two or more cycles. This is the distance-based ICC of Xu, Reiss & Cribben (2021), equivalent for Euclidean distances to I2C2 (Shou et al. 2013).
Earlier check. The same question over 17 features on the between-person scale, with ICC(1) per feature, BCa intervals from 5,000 participant resamples.
No hypothesis tests and no multiplicity adjustment for the cohort contrasts. Estimates come with intervals except where an interval is known to be miscalibrated, which is stated where it happens.
Figures. DABEST forest plots draw each contrast’s bootstrap as a half-violin with the estimate and its 95 % BCa interval. The whorlmap draws the bootstrap of Hedges’ g inside each cell of the feature × contrast grid, the outer ring being the tail nearest zero and the centre the far tail. Colour and axis ranges are set from the plotted values so that no cell saturates, and the range is printed on the figure. Device metrics are blue, symptoms orange, throughout.

title: Methods
text:
Disclosure

Every figure and table pools at least five participants; most pool 24 to 42.
No participant-level value, identifier, calendar date or free-text entry appears in this repository or on this site.
The repeatability and comparison figures are drawn from the cohort-level tables in tables/ by scripts/make_figures.py; the cohort-shift figures are the analysis run’s own, every element a cohort bootstrap. The code that reads the restricted dataset is released from a separate repository after review, as the data licence asks of code behind publications.

title: phaseffect
text:
Interval 2022 of the mcPHASES dataset: 42 participants, Fitbit Sense, Dexcom CGM, Mira urine hormones and a daily diary over about three months. Phases come from the hormone-based labels. Every contrast is within the same participants, against their own follicular days, and is reported as an effect size with a 95 % interval. Nothing on this site is participant-level.


Cohort shifts by phase
Luteal − follicular, same participants: resting heart rate +3.0 bpm [2.2, 3.8], wrist temperature +0.23 °C [0.12, 0.31], glucose +0.16 mmol/L [0.06, 0.27], breathing rate +0.48 /min, HRV −3.9 ms. Menses is the symptom phase: cramps +1.1 points, 41 of 42 participants higher.



Does a person’s shift persist?
The average contrast is clear; whether people differ persistently in it is not settled. Resting heart rate is a candidate: a between-person SD of 1.9 bpm on a 3.0 bpm average, larger than most simulated no-difference cohorts produce. The other four metrics are uninformative. Intervals are withheld until calibrated by simulation.



Methods in one screen · Prior findings on this dataset · aggregate tables in tables/

title: Cohort shifts by phase
text: Positive means higher than on the participant’s own follicular days. Paired mean differences with 95 % bias-corrected bootstrap intervals over 5,000 participant resamples (methods). In the same participants the luteal phase moves five of the six device metrics (sleep duration does not change); menses moves the symptoms. These contrasts agree in direction with published wearable studies (Shilaih et al. 2017; Goodale et al. 2019; Schmalenberger et al. 2019); what is new here is their size, in native units with intervals, for this dataset.

title: Cohort shifts by phase
text:
Standardized, to compare across metrics
Hedges’ g uses the spread of participants’ phase means as its unit, so a consistent 3 bpm shift against baselines that differ by 7 bpm between people scores lower than a one-point symptom shift against baselines that differ by less than a point. Use it to compare cells, not to size an effect.



Whorlmap of Hedges’ g. Each cell spirals its 5,000 bootstrap values from the tail nearest zero (outer ring) to the far tail (centre), 2.5 % trimmed at each end, so a coloured outer ring means the 95 % interval excludes zero. Colour range ±2, set by the widest cell. Rows ordered within each family by its strongest contrast.





The same g with its bootstrap as half-violins, families by contrasts. Each family row has its own scale.





Do two phase contrasts move the same features? One dot per feature. The fertile-window and luteal vectors point the same way; menses is its own direction. Descriptive: features are not independent.

title: Cohort shifts by phase
text:
Read with

Reference phase. The app’s “Follicular” label is the late-follicular phase, from the last day of flow to the first day of the fertile window, the same definition the dataset’s papers use. In this release it is short (median 6 labelled days, against 7.7–11 days in the papers), and the cohort and estimators differ, so agreement with the papers is same-direction, not replication.
Open cycles included. Days in cycles that never closed count towards their labelled phase. Restricted to closed cycles, the luteal contrasts agree for resting heart rate (+3.0 bpm), temperature (+0.28 °C), glucose (+0.21 mmol/L) and breathing rate (+0.53 /min); HRV is smaller there (−2.5 ms against −3.9), so its size depends on that choice.
Multiplicity. 51 cells, no adjustment. 30 exclude zero; two or three would by chance. Symptom cells are strongly correlated with each other.
Not blind. Participants saw the app’s phase predictions while reporting symptoms.
Data handling. 782 of 3,698 resting-heart-rate days were coded 0 and treated as missing; two participants’ glucose was converted from mg/dL; 16 of 3,258 temperature nights were dropped as artefacts.

Table: tables/cohort_phenovector.csv, 51 rows, no identifiers.

title: Prior findings on this dataset
text: Seventeen formal works and about twenty-five repositories touch the dataset. Everything physiological that is published is a pooled group contrast (glucose, wrist temperature, resting heart rate), a classifier score, or a symptom model. For this dataset, no published work reports resting-heart-rate, breathing-rate or HRV phase contrasts in native units, splits a phase contrast into person, cycle and day variation, reports a cross-metric concordance, or anchors an analysis on the 2024 progesterone metabolite (one public code repository has begun to). Within-person luteal changes in these metrics are well established in other wearable studies: sleeping pulse rate (Shilaih et al. 2017), wrist temperature, heart rate, HRV and breathing rate (Goodale et al. 2019), and lower vagal activity in the luteal phase across 37 studies (Schmalenberger et al. 2019). Ribeiro’s 2026 audit has already tested between-person heterogeneity in this dataset, for a different quantity (E3G coupling). This page is the context for the findings here; figures reproduced from other works carry their own licence, stated in the caption.

title: Does a person’s shift persist?
text:
The average contrast is clear; whether people differ persistently in it is not settled. A three-level model of the daily values (person, cycle, day) splits each metric’s luteal contrast into its parts. Resting heart rate is a candidate: its between-person SD, 1.9 bpm on a 3.0 bpm cohort contrast, is larger than most simulated cohorts in which nobody differs produce. The other four metrics are uninformative: for temperature, breathing rate and HRV the model sits on a boundary (a singular fit), and glucose’s estimate is indistinguishable from no difference.

title: Does a person’s shift persist?
text:
The vector across five metrics
Treating each cycle’s five-metric contrast as one vector, the distance-based repeatability index R_vec was 0.07 [−0.11, 0.27] among 22 participants with two or three closed cycles. At this sample size a simulated null spans about ±0.25, and the bootstrap holds the scales fixed, so the interval is too narrow: the index is uninformative.

title: Does a person’s shift persist?
text:
Read with

Two or three cycles per person, over about three months; “persistent” means across consecutive cycles, not years.
Phases are app labels, informed by urinary LH and E3G and carried forward when testing stopped; ovulation is not confirmed in 2022, so a person-level difference could reflect anovulatory cycles or label timing rather than physiology.
Who is counted. The model needs closed cycles; 21 to 31 participants per metric have two or more, which favours regular cyclers.
Sore breasts, the one symptom checked, may also carry a persistent difference; symptoms were reported while participants saw the app’s phase predictions.
Resting heart rate was first flagged by an earlier, cruder check on the same participants (below), so its candidacy is not an independent replication.
Conflicting evidence. In a large WHOOP cohort, the person-to-person spread of a raw resting-heart-rate cycle amplitude was about the same in pill users, who have no hormonal cycle, as in natural cyclers (about 1.9 bpm; Jasinski et al. 2024). Raw spread of that size can be mostly noise, which is why the candidacy here rests on the calibrated null, not on the 1.9 bpm itself.
Method. R_vec is the distance-based ICC of Xu, Reiss & Cribben (2021); recommended designs for random-slope repeatability use far more people and more than two occasions per person, so every estimate here is underpowered.

title: Does a person’s shift persist?
section: The earlier check: 17 features on the between-person scale
text:
The earlier check: 17 features on the between-person scale
Before the model above, a cruder check put all 17 features (six device metrics and eleven symptoms) on a common scale, the between-person spread of phase means, and asked whether a person’s cycle vectors lie closer to each other than to other people’s. They did not: ratio 1.00 [0.92, 1.08] over 24 participants. On that scale a consistent 3 bpm shift against baselines that differ by 7 bpm between people counts for less than a one-point symptom shift, and symptom noise swamps the device metrics. Per feature, resting heart rate had the largest device-metric ICC (0.61 [0.09, 0.86], 14 participants); HRV (0.23 [0.01, 0.61]) and sore breasts (0.53 [0.20, 0.81]) also had intervals above zero, and temperature did not (−0.02 [−0.34, 0.31]). None of these lower limits is a test.



Left: mean distance between a person’s own cycle vectors and to other people’s, 17 features. Right: per-feature ICC of the shift across a person’s cycles.


Tables: tables/rep03_components.csv, tables/rep03_summary.json; the earlier check’s tables/feature_icc.csv and tables/repeatability_summary.json.
